definition: EmoSpark is an artificial intelligence console created in London, United Kingdom by Patrick Levy-Rosenthal.
details: The device uses facial recognition and language analysis to evaluate human emotion and convey responsive content according to the emotion. The console measures 90 mm x 90 mm x 90 mm and is cube shaped. It operates on an "Emotional Processing Unit", an emotion chip developed by Emoshape Inc. that enables the system to create emotional profile graphs of its surroundings. The emotional processing unit is a patent pending technology that is said to create synthesised emotional responses in machines. EmoSpark was funded through an Indiegogo campaign which aimed to raise $200,000.

explainer.lead: EmoSpark is a cube-shaped AI console designed to respond to people’s apparent emotions, not just their words. It combines facial recognition with language analysis and uses an emotion chip to build emotional profile graphs and select responsive content.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a small box that tries to notice whether you seem happy or upset by looking at your face and listening to your words, a bit like a friend reading your mood. It then chooses content to suit that mood. This does not mean the box actually has feelings of its own.
tiers.practitioner: Treat EmoSpark as an emotion-responsive interaction pipeline: facial and language signals feed emotion evaluation, the Emotional Processing Unit builds emotional profile graphs, and the resulting state drives content selection. The console measures 90 mm × 90 mm × 90 mm; the main design pitfall is treating inferred emotions or synthesized responses as reliable readings of a person’s inner state.
tiers.paperLevel: A plain-text abstraction is emotion_state = EPU(face_analysis(face), language_analysis(language)), followed by profile_graph = update(emotion_state) and content = respond(profile_graph). Created in London by Patrick Levy-Rosenthal, the console used an Emoshape Inc. chip described as patent-pending technology for synthesized emotional responses. Its stated ability to synthesize responses is not evidence of subjective machine experience.

explainer.example: If a user smiles while speaking in an upbeat way, EmoSpark can analyze both the face and the language, update its emotional profile, and choose content suited to the positive emotion it infers.

usedIn.name: EmoSpark AI console
usedIn.detail: Uses emotion estimates to convey content responsive to a user’s apparent emotional state.

usedIn.name: Emoshape Emotional Processing Unit
usedIn.detail: The emotion chip inside EmoSpark, used to create emotional profile graphs of its surroundings.

explainer.intuition: The idea is to make a device’s reactions sensitive to emotional context as well as the literal content of speech. EmoSpark treats emotion as an estimated state that can be tracked and used to guide responses.
howItWorks: Facial recognition analyzes a person’s face for emotion-related information.
Language analysis evaluates what the person says.
The Emotional Processing Unit combines these evaluations into an emotional representation.
The system creates emotional profile graphs of its surroundings.
It selects and conveys content responsive to the estimated emotion.
explainer.whyItMatters: EmoSpark illustrates an attempt to make human–machine interaction adaptive to emotional cues rather than limited to commands and text. Its compact console and dedicated emotion chip package that idea as a standalone device.
misconceptions: Synthesizing an emotional response does not show that the machine genuinely feels an emotion.
EmoSpark does not rely on faces alone; language analysis also contributes to its evaluation.
An emotional profile graph is a system-generated representation, not a direct reading of someone’s inner feelings.
